summary: The candidate was referred by an employee and had four rounds. Round 1 covered C basics, electronics and resume projects. Round 2 went into C memory management, Python basics and wireless/cellular communication fundamentals. Round 3 was about certifications and previous jobs, and round 4 was a managerial round. Their tip: if a role matches your profile, you can also send your resume directly to Qualcomm recruiters on LinkedIn.
questions: C basics and electronics questions based on resume projects

summary: Applied through a recruitment agency and had a phone screen with a senior embedded engineer. The discussion focused on debugging with JTAG, interrupts, the difference between hardware and software debugging, and `volatile`. Basic C and RTOS questions followed, including how to implement a round-robin scheduler.
questions: How do you debug with JTAG?
Why is volatile important, and what does extern do?
How would you implement a round-robin scheduler?

summary: A virtual panel with four interviewers, 60 minutes each. Questions centred on multithreading, queues and stacks, bit manipulation and C programming basics. The candidate received an offer and declined it.
questions: Implement or reason about a queue and a stack

summary: Reports on this page describe three one-hour rounds: a principal engineer mixing phone-screen questions with easy C questions, a senior engineer walking through the resume and then two coding questions, and another senior engineer round. Pointer arithmetic came up early. One recruiter-sourced candidate advises knowing every project on your resume well and expecting behavioural questions.
questions: Implement a calculator without if/else, switch or loops
Two coding questions after a resume walkthrough

summary: A first-round phone screen of about 50 minutes: roughly 10 minutes on the resume, 30 minutes of Linux kernel questions and 10 minutes of C. Most questions were short yes/no style but tricky, so precise understanding mattered more than long explanations.
questions: Top half vs bottom half of an ISR

summary: Two phone interviews with coding challenges, computer architecture, Linux and protocol questions. The candidate was then invited onsite for a full loop of 6–7 interviews from 9:30am to 4pm, some focused purely on coding skills.
The interview opened with a detailed project discussion, then moved to core OS questions and a C++ coding problem, followed by Linux and system-call questions.
Many technical questions: short programs and algorithms, some maths, Linux kernel internals and basic hardware debugging. Another report on the same page describes an interval problem.
questions: Calculate the angle between clock hands
Implement aligned malloc and aligned free
Given (start, end) intervals, find the busiest hour

summary: Applied online. The process was a take-home coding test followed by four onsite rounds focused on embedded programming. The candidate accepted the offer.

Technical rounds covered operating systems, RTOS, data structures, multithreading, bit manipulation, BIOS and bootloaders, plus coding rounds on strings and bits. Hiring manager and HR rounds followed before the offer.

A phone interview on C and firmware knowledge, followed by two on-site technical interviews of about two hours each, solving three LeetCode-style problems on a whiteboard. A Bengaluru intern report on the same page mentions cache coherence and memory hierarchy questions.
questions: Three LeetCode-style problems on a board

summary: One hour: about 15 minutes on the resume and projects, then three coding questions on CoderPad, one of them counting the set bits in a number. A separate intern report on the same page lists structure padding, volatile and interrupt questions, and advises expecting bit manipulation, pointers and memory, and linked lists.
questions: Count the set bits in a number
Two more short coding questions on CoderPad

summary: Two technical interviews of one hour each, split into 30 minutes of questions and 30 minutes of live coding. Many questions covered embedded systems basics, intermediate C and the candidate's project experience.
Two levels. The first covered C programming, project basics and Linux fundamentals; the second went into Linux kernel driver programming and previous experience. The candidate was selected.

The role description was broad (years of C++, embedded background, strong debugging). The live coding question was very practical: unpacking raw sensor-style data stored as packed 12-bit values in padded rows. The candidate found the overall process frustrating.
questions: Move packed 12-bit integers stored in 64-byte padded rows into an NxM matrix of 16-bit values
What is a mutex? (from another report on the page)

summary: A sequence of classic coding problems adapted to firmware style, ending with a concurrency question.
questions: Sort colours where elements are objects with a colour field

summary: A 30-minute recruiter screen about the resume, then a one-hour technical interview with the hiring manager on the resume, C basics and debugging techniques, followed by a take-home with two coding questions.

Questions on embedded software basics, HAL and BSP design and expert-level C, mostly built around the candidate's own projects and experience. The candidate found the questions very relevant to real firmware work and accepted the offer.
Referred by an employee; the process took about three weeks. Four rounds in total: one phone/video call and three technical rounds of coding and embedded-systems questions.

The first round was a recorded HireVue interview: two behavioural STAR questions and a coding challenge that the candidate recognised as an old programming-competition problem about decoding messages.
questions: Introduce yourself and explain why Boeing

summary: Mostly STAR-based behavioural questions and questions taken from the resume, with a single technical question.
questions: Explain an RTOS in detail and its use cases

summary: A telephone round of about an hour focused on CAN and Embedded C, then a face-to-face round on current work, CAN, Embedded C, C++ and automotive technology, followed by a senior manager and HR. The candidate found everyone friendly.

A design-style technical round on integrating a temperature sensor and building the RTOS application, C questions, and some AUTOSAR background expected. The managerial round covered past work, challenges and how they were overcome.
questions: How would you integrate a temperature sensor and develop the RTOS application?

summary: Campus process with a single online interview round and two interviewers. Questions were based on projects, microcontrollers and C; embedded projects on the resume drew detailed questions.
questions: Predict the output of C snippets

summary: An online assessment with C questions, then a technical interview on embedded systems, projects, C and computer architecture, and an HR round asking why the candidate wanted an embedded role rather than a general software one.

Campus hiring for an internship plus full-time role. The online assessment was one hour of MCQs on C and OS with a strong focus on pointer arithmetic and negative marking. The first interview was an elimination round on the resume and core subjects, even though the candidate's background was mostly general software.
questions: Rate yourself in C, C++ and Python

summary: Applied online; the process took about three days. Questions covered C/C++, memory management, algorithms and data structures, bitwise operators, preprocessor directives and optimisation, plus background and experience.
questions: Where in memory are the variables in this code stored?

summary: The first round at Samsung Semiconductor India Research was three coding questions in 90 minutes, ranging from easy to medium. Later rounds followed for shortlisted candidates.
Applied online; the process took about three months. One memorable question gave five or six short C functions and asked which compiler optimisations could or could not be applied to each.
questions: Explain which compiler optimisations are legal for each of several short C functions

summary: Core OS and architecture questions for a firmware internship.
